text: How would you guess the price of a flat you have never seen? Most people would look at similar flats nearby and assume this one costs about the same. That instinct is a complete machine learning method, called k nearest neighbours. It learns no weights at all; it simply remembers every example, and when a new question arrives, it looks for the most similar examples it has stored.

Similar needs a definition, and the usual one is distance. Each example is a point, a vector of features, and the distance between two points is the length of the arrow from one to the other, the norm of their difference, which you already know how to compute. For a new point we measure the distance to every stored example, sort them, and keep the k closest.

What happens next depends on the question. For classification, the neighbours vote, and the new point takes the most common label among them. For a number such as a price, we take the average of the neighbours' values. That is the whole algorithm; all the cleverness lies in choosing k and in choosing what distance means.

Choosing k is the bias and variance trade-off again. With k equal to one, every point trusts a single neighbour, so the boundary between classes becomes jagged, wrapping around every stray noisy point; that is high variance. As k grows, the vote smooths the boundary out. Push k too far and the vote is dominated by whichever class is most common overall, so the model stops seeing local structure at all, which is high bias. We pick k with a validation set.

Distance also hides a trap. Suppose one feature is floor area in square metres and another is the number of bedrooms. Area spans hundreds, bedrooms span a handful, so area dominates every distance and bedrooms barely count, purely because of the units we chose. The cure is to standardise each feature to a similar scale before measuring distance, using statistics from the training set.

Nearest neighbours pays for skipping training at prediction time, since every query is compared with every stored point. It also weakens in high dimensions: as the number of features grows, the distances between random points become more and more alike, so the nearest neighbour is hardly nearer than the farthest. Researchers call this the curse of dimensionality.

Yet nearest neighbour search is at the heart of retrieval augmented generation. Your documents are turned into embedding vectors, your question becomes another vector, and a vector database returns the stored chunks closest to it, usually by cosine similarity and with clever approximate search, so that the language model can read them. Next, we turn to decision trees, which learn a sequence of questions instead.
